n: Light is created on the first day, the sun and moon only on the fourth. Readers ancient and modern have noticed. The text is arranged as a week of work — three days of separating (light, waters, land), three of filling (lights, fish and birds, animals and humans) — a liturgical poem, not a laboratory report.

Three hundred cubits long (about 135 metres), with three decks and a single door — a floating box, not a ship, with no rudder: God steers. Mesopotamia had older flood stories (Gilgamesh, Atrahasis); Genesis retells the theme with one just God instead of quarrelling ones. 1 Peter 3:20 makes the ark a picture of baptism.

t: Noe's drunkenness and the curse of Chanaan
n: The first vineyard, the first drunkenness. Noe curses not Cham, who saw him naked, but Cham's son Chanaan — a text written to explain Israel's later dominance over the Canaanites. Its abuse to justify the enslavement of Africans is one of the darkest chapters in the history of biblical interpretation.

Fire and brimstone on the cities of the plain, and Lot's wife turned to salt for looking back. Jesus' three-word warning, 'Remember Lot's wife' (Luke 17:32), makes her the type of the person who cannot let go. The Dead Sea's salt formations still bear her name for tourists.

'The voice indeed is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau.' A blind father, a scheming mother, goat-skins on the arms — and a blessing that, once spoken, cannot be recalled. The Bible does not excuse the deceit; Jacob will be deceived in turn by Laban (chapter 29) and by his own sons (chapter 37).

'They seemed but a few days, because of the greatness of his love.' Then the trick: in the morning it is Lia (Leah). The deceiver is deceived, and works seven more years. The two sisters and their maids will bear the twelve tribes; Rachel's tomb near Bethlehem is still a pilgrimage site.

A widow denied the husband owed her by custom dresses as a prostitute and conceives twins by her father-in-law Juda. When he moves to burn her, she produces his seal and staff, and he admits: 'she is juster than I'. Matthew's genealogy names her, unembarrassed, among Jesus' ancestors.

The Hebrew word for the basket is the same as for Noe's ark — a small ark on the Nile. Pharaoh's own daughter rescues the child his decree condemned, and his mother is paid to nurse him. 'Moses' is an Egyptian name (as in Thut-mose); the text hears the Hebrew 'drawn out'.

Blood, frogs, gnats, flies, cattle plague, boils, hail, locusts, darkness, death of the firstborn. Each strikes something Egypt worshipped — the Nile, the sun, Pharaoh's own divine line. Ten times Pharaoh's heart is hardened, sometimes by himself, sometimes by God: the text holds both without resolving it.

At Raphidim the people quarrel and Moses strikes the rock. Paul says startlingly, 'they drank of the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ' (1 Cor 10:4). The place is named Massa and Meriba, 'testing' and 'quarrel' — Psalm 94 warns, 'harden not your hearts as at Meriba'.

A gold-covered chest holding the tablets, with two cherubim on its lid — the 'propitiatory' or mercy seat, where God promises 'I will speak to thee'. It went before Israel into battle, was captured by the Philistines, brought to Jerusalem by David, and vanished when Babylon burned the Temple. Its fate is unknown.

t: 'As a man is wont to speak to his friend'
n: The Lord spoke to Moses 'face to face, as a man is wont to speak to his friend'. No other figure in the Old Testament is given this intimacy — and yet a few verses later Moses cannot see God's face and live. Both are true: friendship, and unbridgeable distance.

Cloven hoof and chewing the cud: the origin of kosher law. Explanations range from hygiene to symbolism — creatures that fit their category cleanly are 'clean'. Jesus 'made all meats clean' (Mark 7:19) and Peter's vision in Acts 10 opens the table to Gentiles; observant Jews keep the rules to this day.

t: 'Be ye holy, because I the Lord your God am holy'
n: The refrain of the 'Holiness Code' (Leviticus 17–26). Holiness means set apart, belonging to God — and the chapter that follows applies it to harvest gleanings for the poor, honest weights, wages paid on time, and not cursing the deaf. 1 Peter 1:16 quotes the verse for Christians.

Twelve spies, forty days, a cluster of grapes so large two men carry it on a pole — and then panic: 'we seemed like locusts'. Only Caleb and Josue trust God. The whole generation is condemned to die in the desert; the forty years of wandering follow from this one night of fear.

t: 'A star shall rise out of Jacob'
n: Balaam's final oracle: 'a star shall rise out of Jacob and a sceptre shall spring up from Israel'. Jews applied it to David and later to Bar Kochba ('son of the star'), leader of the revolt of AD 132; Christians to the Magi's star. It appears on the coins of the Jewish revolt.

Deuteronomy means 'second law': Moses on the plains of Moab retelling Sinai to the children of those who stood there. The Sabbath commandment here is grounded not in creation, as in Exodus, but in the Exodus — 'remember that thou also didst serve in Egypt'. Rest is a freedom you were denied.

Fourteen verses of blessing, fifty-four of curse: siege, famine, exile, 'thou shalt be scattered among all people'. The exiles of 586 BC read this chapter as their own history foretold, which is why Deuteronomy shaped the books of Kings. The theology — obey and prosper — is what Job argues against.

A woman judges Israel under a palm tree and leads it to war; another, Jahel, hammers a tent-peg through the fleeing general's skull. Chapter 5, the Song of Debbora, is among the oldest poetry in the Bible. Judges is a spiral of decline — 'every one did that which seemed right to himself' — and its heroes are increasingly flawed.

Saul keeps the best sheep of Amalec 'to sacrifice to the Lord' and is rejected as king for it. Samuel's answer became a prophetic slogan: God wants obedience, not offerings. From here Saul's decline is unstoppable — jealousy, madness, the witch of Endor, death on Gelboe.

Forbidden by his own law, Saul consults a medium the night before his last battle and the ghost of Samuel rises, furious, to announce his death. Theologians argued whether it was really Samuel or a demon; the text takes it as Samuel. It is the Bible's only séance, told with dread.

t: David's lament for Saul and Jonathan
n: 'How are the valiant fallen!' — David mourns the king who hunted him and the friend who loved him 'beyond the love of women'. He orders it taught to Judah as the Song of the Bow. It is grief without a word of triumph; Israel's greatest king begins his reign by weeping for his rival.

t: 'My son Absalom, would God I might die for thee'
n: Absalom rebelled against his father, and David's men killed him against orders as he hung by his hair from an oak. The king's grief — 'Absalom my son, my son' — is the rawest cry of a parent in the Bible. The fathers saw a father who would die in his son's place; Faulkner took his title from it.

'If heaven and the heavens of heavens cannot contain thee, how much less this house?' Solomon's prayer knows the paradox of a God who fills everything choosing one place to be found. The Temple (about 960 BC) stood four centuries; its site is the Temple Mount, where the Dome of the Rock now stands.

A foreign widow with a handful of meal and a little oil shares her last meal with the prophet, and neither runs out through the famine. Jesus cites her, with Naaman, to say God's favour has always crossed borders — and Nazareth tries to throw him off a cliff for it (Luke 4:26).

Naboth will not sell his ancestral vineyard; Queen Jezabel arranges false witnesses and a stoning. Elias meets Achab in the vineyard: 'Hast thou killed, and also taken possession?' The prophets' role in Israel — confronting kings over land and blood — is nowhere clearer.

t: The book found in the Temple
n: Repairs to the Temple under King Josias (622 BC) turn up 'the book of the law' — probably a form of Deuteronomy — and the young king tears his garments on hearing it read. The reform that followed centralised worship in Jerusalem and shaped how the rest of the Old Testament was edited.

t: 'As the hart panteth after the fountains of water'
n: Psalm 41 (Hebrew 42) opens the second book of the Psalter with an exile's homesickness for the Temple: 'my soul hath thirsted after the strong living God'. It was sung as the newly baptised approached the font at Easter, and deer drinking at streams decorate early Christian baptisteries.

Psalm 83 (Hebrew 84): a pilgrim's psalm, in love with the Temple courts, envying the sparrow that nests near the altar. 'Better is one day in thy courts above thousands.' Brahms set it in the German Requiem.

Psalm 94 (Hebrew 95) opens the Church's daily prayer every morning: 'Come let us praise the Lord with joy'. Its second half turns to warning — 'today if you shall hear his voice, harden not your hearts' — which Hebrews 3–4 develops into a whole sermon on 'today'.

t: 'As a father hath compassion on his children'
n: Psalm 102 (Hebrew 103): 'as far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our iniquities from us... he knoweth our frame, he remembereth that we are dust'. The psalm quotes Exodus 34's 'merciful and gracious' and turns it into song.

t: 'Lord, thou hast proved me, and known me'
n: Psalm 138 (Hebrew 139): the psalm of God's inescapable presence — 'if I ascend into heaven, thou art there; if I descend into hell, thou art present' — and of God knitting the psalmist in the womb. Its meditation on being known has made it a favourite of contemplatives and of those praying for the unborn.

'Have confidence in the Lord with all thy heart... in all thy ways think on him, and he will direct thy steps.' Among the most memorised verses in the Bible. Proverbs 1–9 is a father's instruction to a son, framing the short sayings that follow.

t: Old age as a house falling in
n: 'Remember thy Creator in the days of thy youth' opens the Bible's most beautiful description of aging: the keepers of the house tremble (arms), the grinders are few (teeth), the windows darken (eyes), the almond tree flowers (white hair), 'and the dust return into its earth... and the spirit return to God'.

'For winter is now past, the rain is over and gone. The flowers have appeared in our land.' The Song's most quoted lyric — spring as the season of love. Monastic writers heard Christ calling the soul; the Church reads it on the feast of the Visitation.

Twenty-one attributes of Wisdom (three times seven): 'a vapour of the power of God... the brightness of eternal light, and the unspotted mirror of God's majesty'. Hebrews 1:3 describes the Son in these terms. Together with Proverbs 8 and Sirach 24 this is the Old Testament root of the doctrine of the Word.

Sirach expands the fourth commandment into a whole chapter: care for a father in old age, 'and if his understanding fail, have patience with him'. It is read on the feast of the Holy Family. Sirach is the most 'practical' book of the Bible, on everything from table manners to lending money.

t: Wisdom pitches her tent in Israel
n: Wisdom, who 'came out of the mouth of the most High' and circled heaven and earth, is told by the Creator: 'Let thy dwelling be in Jacob'. She becomes the Law of Moses (24:32). John 1:14, 'the Word was made flesh and dwelt (pitched his tent) among us', echoes this chapter. The Church applies it to the Virgin Mary.

t: 'They shall turn their swords into ploughshares'
n: All nations stream to the mountain of the Lord's house; war is unlearned. The words are carved outside the United Nations. Micheas 4 has the same oracle almost word for word; Joel 3 reverses it ('beat your ploughshares into swords') — the Bible arguing with itself about the last days.

t: The feast on the mountain, death destroyed
n: 'A feast of fat things, a feast of wine... he shall cast death down headlong for ever, and the Lord God shall wipe away tears from every face.' Revelation 21:4 quotes this; it is read at funerals and gives the Mass its image of the heavenly banquet.

t: 'All you that thirst, come to the waters'
n: Free wine and milk, 'without money and without any price'; God's thoughts higher than ours 'as the heavens are exalted above the earth'; and the word that 'shall not return to me void' but does what it was sent for. The chapter closes the Book of Consolation and is read at the Easter Vigil.

Not bowing the head like a bulrush, but loosing the bands of wickedness, feeding the hungry, housing the homeless — 'then shall thy light break forth as the morning'. The Church reads this on the Friday after Ash Wednesday, to say at the start of Lent what fasting is for.

Jeremias' most intimate complaint: God has seduced (the Hebrew is that strong) and overpowered him; he is a daily laughing-stock; yet when he tries to stop, the word is 'a burning fire shut up in my bones'. No prophet argues with God more bitterly or stays more faithful.

Build houses, plant gardens, marry, 'seek the peace of the city to which I have caused you to be carried away' — and after seventy years I will bring you back. Jeremias tells the exiles to settle in Babylon instead of waiting for quick rescue; verse 11, 'thoughts of peace and not of affliction', is one of the most quoted in Scripture.

After denouncing Israel's leaders as shepherds who feed themselves, God announces that he will shepherd the flock personally — seeking the lost, binding the broken. Jesus' 'I am the good shepherd' (John 10) and the parable of the lost sheep are this chapter made flesh.

t: 'A new heart... a heart of flesh'
n: 'I will pour upon you clean water... and I will give you a new heart, and put a new spirit within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh.' Water, heart, spirit — the vocabulary of baptism. Read at the Easter Vigil beside the font.

Gold, silver, brass, iron mixed with clay — four empires, then a stone 'cut out of a mountain without hands' that shatters them and fills the earth. Daniel's scheme of successive kingdoms shaped Jewish and Christian views of history for two thousand years; the stone was read as Christ's kingdom.

Baltassar drinks from the Temple vessels at a feast; fingers write on the plaster. Daniel reads: Mane, Thecel, Phares — numbered, weighed, divided. 'Thou art weighed in the balance, and art found wanting.' That night Babylon falls (539 BC). The English idiom 'the writing on the wall' comes from here.

Trapped by a law his rivals engineered, Daniel keeps praying toward Jerusalem three times a day and is thrown to the lions; the king cannot sleep, and finds him unharmed at dawn. The story was among the earliest painted in the catacombs — a Christian facing the arena saw himself in it.

Jesus quotes this verse twice in Matthew (9:13, 12:7), each time to Pharisees: 'go and learn what this meaneth'. Hebrew hesed — loyal love, covenant kindness — is what God wants more than ritual. Osee's whole book is about love that keeps going after betrayal.

t: A famine of hearing the word
n: 'Not a famine of bread, nor a thirst of water, but of hearing the word of the Lord.' Amos threatens the worst punishment: silence from God. His book ends (9:11–15) with the fallen tent of David rebuilt — a passage James quotes at the Council of Jerusalem to admit the Gentiles (Acts 15:16).

A century after Jonas, Nineveh has not stayed repentant. Nahum exults over its destruction (612 BC) — 'behold upon the mountains the feet of him that bringeth good tidings', a line Isaias 52 and Romans 10 also use. The Bible keeps both books: mercy for Nineveh and judgment on it.

t: 'Although the fig tree shall not blossom'
n: Habacuc's closing prayer: crops fail, flocks vanish, 'but I will rejoice in the Lord'. Faith with nothing left to lean on. The verse has comforted farmers and the bereaved alike; the chapter is a psalm, complete with musical directions.

t: 'The Lord thy God in the midst of thee is mighty'
n: After two chapters of the 'day of the Lord' — Sophonias gave the Church the Dies iræ — the book turns to joy: 'he will rejoice over thee with gladness... he will be silent in his love'. Read on the third Sunday of Advent (Gaudete) and, by Luke's echo, behind Gabriel's greeting to Mary.

t: 'The desired of all nations shall come'
n: Aggeus urges the returned exiles (520 BC) to rebuild the Temple; to those who remember Solomon's, the new one looks like nothing. God promises: 'the glory of this last house shall be greater than the first'. Jerome's 'the desired of all nations' became a title of Christ and an Advent hymn.

t: 'They shall look upon me, whom they have pierced'
n: A mysterious oracle of mourning over one pierced, 'as one mourneth for an only son'. John 19:37 quotes it as the soldier's spear enters Jesus' side, and Revelation 1:7 makes it the watchword of the Second Coming. Zacharias 9–14 is quoted in the passion narratives more than any other prophet except Isaias.

'From the rising of the sun even to the going down, my name is great among the Gentiles, and in every place there is sacrifice, and there is offered to my name a clean oblation.' From the second century the Church read this as a prophecy of the Eucharist offered worldwide; it is quoted in the Roman Canon's tradition.

'Behold I send my angel, and he shall prepare the way before my face' — 'Malachias' means 'my messenger', so the prophet's name is his message. Jesus applies the verse to John the Baptist (Matt 11:10); 'the Lord whom you seek shall suddenly come to his temple' is read on Candlemas, when the infant is carried in.

Old Tobias's advice to his son: give according to your means, 'turn not away thy face from any poor person', for 'alms deliver from all sin and from death'. This is the Old Testament source of the Jewish and Catholic conviction that charity has power before God; the Golden Rule appears in its negative form at 4:16.

Sackcloth, ashes, and a prayer that God is 'the God of the humble, the helper of the little ones... the saviour of them that are without hope'. Judith goes to war armed with beauty and this prayer. Her thanksgiving song (chapter 16) echoes Debbora's, and Mary's Magnificat echoes both.

Found only in the Greek additions (Vulgate chapter 14), Esther strips off her royal robes, covers her head with ashes and prays: 'O my Lord, who alone art our king, help me a desolate woman'. It supplies what the Hebrew Esther left unsaid — that her courage was prayed for first.

The village women name the child Obed, 'father of Isai, the father of David'. The book's last word is 'David': a story of two widows gleaning barley turns out to be the beginning of the royal line — and, through Matthew 1, of Jesus. Booz the redeemer became a type of Christ.

t: 'Man born of a woman, living for a short time'
n: 'Cometh forth like a flower, and is destroyed, and fleeth as a shadow.' Job's meditation on mortality; the Book of Common Prayer put it in the burial service. The chapter goes on to ask, 'Shall man that is dead live again?' — and cannot yet answer.

A poem on mining — men dig for silver, sapphires, gold in the dark — that turns to ask where wisdom is mined. Not in the sea, not for gold; 'God understandeth the way of it'. The answer given to man is only: 'the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom'. The Bible's most beautiful poem about the limits of knowledge.
